title: State-Space Models
description: Write differential equations, circuits and mechanical systems as state equations, and get the transfer function back.

study.title: Why state space?
study.body:
Year 2 control described each loop by one transfer function. State space keeps the inside of the system: $n$ **state variables** that, together with the input from now on, fix the whole future. The model is $n$ first-order equations in matrix form. It handles several inputs and outputs and leads to designs that place **all** closed-loop poles at once.
- $\mathbf{A}$ ($n\times n$): how the states drive each other
- $\mathbf{B}$ ($n\times m$): how the $m$ inputs enter
- $\mathbf{C}$ ($p\times n$) and $\mathbf{D}$ ($p\times m$): what the $p$ outputs measure

study.title: From a differential equation
study.body: Take the output and its derivatives as states: $x_1 = y$, $x_2 = \dot y$, … Each state is the derivative of the one before, and the last row is the ODE solved for the highest derivative. First divide by the leading coefficient. **Example:** $2\ddot y + 10\dot y + 12y = 4u$ becomes $\ddot y = -6y - 5\dot y + 2u$, so with $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$ and $D = 0$:

study.title: Mechanical systems
study.body: Masses store kinetic energy and springs potential energy, so the states are **positions and velocities**. A mass $m$ on a spring $k$ with a damper $b$, pushed by a force $F$, obeys $m\ddot p + b\dot p + kp = F$. With $x_1 = p$ and $x_2 = \dot p$ you get the model below. Measuring the position gives $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$, measuring the velocity $\mathbf{C} = [0 \;\; 1]$.

study.title: Circuits: an RC ladder
study.body: Capacitor voltages and inductor currents are the states. Write KCL at each capacitor ($C\dot v$ = net current in) and KVL around each inductor ($L\dot i$ = voltage across it), and keep only states and sources on the right. For the ladder: $C_1\dot v_1 = \frac{v_s - v_1}{R_1} - \frac{v_1 - v_2}{R_2}$ and $C_2\dot v_2 = \frac{v_1 - v_2}{R_2}$. With conductances $G_i = 1/R_i$:

study.title: Control and observer canonical forms
study.body:
A transfer function can be realized straight from its coefficients. Make the denominator **monic** first. For $G(s) = \frac{b_1s + b_2}{s^2 + a_1s + a_2}$:
- **Control canonical form**: the negated denominator coefficients fill the **top row** of $\mathbf{A}_c$, $\mathbf{B}_c = [1 \;\; 0]^T$, and the numerator gives $\mathbf{C}_c = [b_1 \;\; b_2]$.
- **Observer canonical form**: the transpose, $\mathbf{A}_o = \mathbf{A}_c^T = \begin{bmatrix} -a_1 & 1 \\ -a_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B}_o = \mathbf{C}_c^T$, $\mathbf{C}_o = \mathbf{B}_c^T$.
The phase-variable form of Discrete-Time Signals & Systems is the control canonical form with the states numbered in reverse. In the diagram each integrator output is a state; higher orders work the same way.

study.title: Transfer function from a state model
study.body:
Laplace-transform with zero initial state: $s\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{B}U$, so $\mathbf{X} = (s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B}U$. The denominator is $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})$: the poles are the **eigenvalues** of $\mathbf{A}$. For 2×2 use the adjugate (swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal) over the determinant.
**Example:** $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$. Then $\mathrm{adj}(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\,\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ s+1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\det(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}) = (s+1)(s+2)$, so $G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}$.

study.title: Block diagram of a state model
study.body: The integrator $1/s$ turns $\dot{\mathbf{x}}$ into $\mathbf{x}$. $\mathbf{A}$ feeds the states back to the integrator input, $\mathbf{B}$ injects the input, $\mathbf{C}$ forms the output and $D$ is a direct path that skips the dynamics. With $D \ne 0$ the output reacts instantly to a step in $u$.

steps.title: State variables
steps.body: The **state** is the smallest set of variables that, together with the input from now on, fixes the future of the system. Natural choices are the energy stores: capacitor voltages, inductor currents, positions and velocities. An $n$th-order system has $n$ states. Collected in a vector $\mathbf{x}$, they obey $n$ first-order equations.

steps.prompt: A system has $n$ = {{n}} states, $m$ = {{m}} input(s) and $p$ = {{p}} outputs. What is the size of $\mathbf{B}$ (rows × columns)?
steps.explanation: $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}$ is added to $\dot{\mathbf{x}}$, so it has {{n}} rows; it multiplies $\mathbf{u}$ with {{m}} entries, so it has {{m}} columns: {{n}} × {{m}}. Likewise $\mathbf{A}$ is {{n}} × {{n}}, $\mathbf{C}$ is {{p}} × {{n}} and $\mathbf{D}$ is {{p}} × {{m}}.

steps.title: From an ODE to state form
steps.body: Take the output and its derivatives as states. For $\ddot y + a_1\dot y + a_0y = b\,u$ choose $x_1 = y$ and $x_2 = \dot y$. Then $\dot x_1 = x_2$ (by definition) and $\dot x_2 = \ddot y = -a_0x_1 - a_1x_2 + bu$ (the ODE solved for the highest derivative). Measuring $y$ gives $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$.

steps.prompt: Write ${{q}}\ddot y + {{c1}}\dot y + {{c0}}y = {{d}}u$ in state form with $x_1 = y$, $x_2 = \dot y$.

ask.explanation: Divide by {{q}}: $\ddot y = -\frac{{{c0}}}{{{q}}}y - \frac{{{c1}}}{{{q}}}\dot y + \frac{{{d}}}{{{q}}}u$. Row 2 of $\mathbf{A}$ holds the coefficients of $x_1 = y$ and $x_2 = \dot y$, so $a_{21} = -{{c0}}/{{q}}$ = {{-c0/q}}.
Divide by {{q}}: $\ddot y = -\frac{{{c0}}}{{{q}}}y - \frac{{{c1}}}{{{q}}}\dot y + \frac{{{d}}}{{{q}}}u$. The coefficient of $x_2 = \dot y$ is $a_{22} = -{{c1}}/{{q}}$ = {{-c1/q}}.

Divide by {{q}}: $\ddot y = \ldots + \frac{{{d}}}{{{q}}}u$. The input only appears in the $\dot x_2$ equation, so $b_1 = 0$ and $b_2$ = {{d}}/{{q}} = {{d/q}}. Forgetting to divide by the leading coefficient is the classic mistake.

steps.prompt: A {{m}} kg mass on a spring ($k$ = {{k}} N/m) with a damper ($b$ = {{b}} N·s/m) is pushed by a force $F$. States: $x_1 = p$ (position) and $x_2 = \dot p$ (velocity); input $u = F$.

ask.explanation: Newton: $m\ddot p = F - kp - b\dot p$, so $\dot x_2 = -\frac{k}{m}x_1 - \frac{b}{m}x_2 + \frac{1}{m}F$. $a_{21} = -k/m$ = −{{k}}/{{m}} = {{-k/m}}.
Newton: $m\ddot p = F - kp - b\dot p$, so $\dot x_2 = -\frac{k}{m}x_1 - \frac{b}{m}x_2 + \frac{1}{m}F$. $a_{22} = -b/m$ = −{{b}}/{{m}} = {{-b/m}}.
Newton: $m\ddot p = F - kp - b\dot p$, so the force enters as $\frac{1}{m}F$ in $\dot x_2$: $b_2 = 1/m$ = {{1/m}} (and $b_1 = 0$, because $\dot x_1 = x_2$ does not involve $F$).

steps.prompt: Match each matrix to its role.
pairs: How the states drive each other
How the input enters the state equations
Which combination of states is measured
Direct path from input to output
steps.explanation: $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{B}u$: $\mathbf{A}$ couples the states (its eigenvalues are the poles), $\mathbf{B}$ says where the input pushes. $y = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{x} + Du$: $\mathbf{C}$ picks what the sensor sees, and $D$ passes the input straight through without any dynamics (often 0 for physical plants).

steps.title: Circuits
steps.body: In a circuit the energy stores give the states: one voltage per capacitor, one current per inductor. Write $C\dot v_C$ = (current into the capacitor) from KCL and $L\dot i_L$ = (voltage across the inductor) from KVL. Then express every current and voltage on the right in terms of states and sources only.

steps.prompt: For the RC ladder with states $v_1$, $v_2$ (across $C_1$, $C_2$) and input $v_s$: $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, $C_1$ = {{C1|F}}, $C_2$ = {{C2|F}}.

ask.explanation: KCL at $C_1$: $C_1\dot v_1 = \frac{v_s - v_1}{R_1} - \frac{v_1 - v_2}{R_2}$. The coefficient of $v_2$ is $+\frac{1}{R_2C_1}$ = 1/({{R2|Ω}} × {{C1|F}}) = {{1/(R2*C1)}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
KCL at $C_2$: $C_2\dot v_2 = \frac{v_1 - v_2}{R_2}$. The coefficient of $v_1$ is $\frac{1}{R_2C_2}$ = 1/({{R2|Ω}} × {{C2|F}}) = {{1/(R2*C2)}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
The source only drives $C_1$ through $R_1$: $C_1\dot v_1 = \frac{v_s}{R_1} + \ldots$, so $b_1 = \frac{1}{R_1C_1}$ = {{1/(R1*C1)}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (and $b_2 = 0$).

steps.prompt: Every system has exactly one correct state-space model.
steps.explanation: Any invertible change of variables $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{T}\mathbf{z}$ gives another valid model with the same input-output behaviour: you can scale a state (millimetres instead of metres), reorder the states, or mix them. The canonical forms are just convenient standard choices. What is fixed is the transfer function and, for a minimal model, the number of states.

steps.title: Control canonical form
steps.body: A transfer function can be turned into a state model by reading off its coefficients. With a **monic** denominator $s^2 + a_1s + a_2$ and numerator $b_1s + b_2$, the control canonical form puts the negated denominator coefficients in the top row of $\mathbf{A}_c$. The input enters only the first integrator, and the numerator coefficients weight the states in the output: $\mathbf{C}_c = [b_1 \;\; b_2]$.

steps.prompt: Which $\mathbf{A}$, together with $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{C} = [{{b1}} \;\; {{b2}}]$, realizes $G(s) = \frac{{{b1}}s + {{b2}}}{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$?
steps.explanation: This is the control canonical form: top row $[-a_1 \;\; -a_2]$ = [−{{a1}}  −{{a2}}] in rising order of the subscript, and $[1 \;\; 0]$ below it ($\dot x_2 = x_1$). Then $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}$. Positive signs would give poles in the right half-plane, swapped coefficients the wrong polynomial, and the bottom-row (phase-variable) layout only works with $\mathbf{B} = [0 \;\; 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{C} = [b_2 \;\; b_1]$.

steps.title: Observer canonical form
steps.body: Transposing gives a second standard realization: $\mathbf{A}_o = \mathbf{A}_c^T$, $\mathbf{B}_o = \mathbf{C}_c^T$, $\mathbf{C}_o = \mathbf{B}_c^T$. Now the numerator enters through $\mathbf{B}_o$ and the output is simply the first state, $\mathbf{C}_o = [1 \;\; 0]$. The transfer function is the same, because $G(s)$ is a scalar and equals its own transpose.

steps.prompt: Realize $G(s) = \frac{{{n1}}s + {{n0}}}{{{k}}s^2 + {{k*a1}}s + {{k*a2}}}$ in observer canonical form.

ask.explanation: First make the denominator monic: divide top and bottom by {{k}}, giving $\frac{ {{n1/k}}s + {{n0/k}} }{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$. The first column of $\mathbf{A}_o$ is $[-a_1 \;\; -a_2]^T$, so the bottom-left entry is −{{a2}}.
Divide top and bottom by {{k}}: $\frac{ {{n1/k}}s + {{n0/k}} }{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$. $\mathbf{B}_o = [b_1 \;\; b_2]^T$ holds the numerator, so the top entry is $b_1$ = {{n1}}/{{k}} = {{n1/k}}.
Divide top and bottom by {{k}}: $\frac{ {{n1/k}}s + {{n0/k}} }{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$. $\mathbf{B}_o = [b_1 \;\; b_2]^T$, so the bottom entry is $b_2$ = {{n0}}/{{k}} = {{n0/k}}.

steps.prompt: The control and the observer canonical form of the same $G(s)$ have the same eigenvalues.
steps.explanation: $\mathbf{A}_o = \mathbf{A}_c^T$, and a matrix and its transpose have the same characteristic polynomial: $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}^T) = \det\big((s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^T\big) = \det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})$. Both have the poles of $G(s)$ as eigenvalues.

steps.title: Back to a transfer function
steps.body: For a 2×2 model, $(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} = \frac{1}{\Delta(s)}\begin{bmatrix} s - a_{22} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & s - a_{11} \end{bmatrix}$ with $\Delta(s) = s^2 - \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A})\,s + \det\mathbf{A}$. The numerator is $\mathbf{C}\,\mathrm{adj}(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})\,\mathbf{B}$. With $\mathbf{B} = [1 \;\; 0]^T$ only the first column of the adjugate matters.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a11}} & {{a12}} \\ {{a21}} & {{a22}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [{{c1}} \;\; {{c2}}]$, $D = 0$. Write $G(s) = \frac{\beta_1s + \beta_0}{s^2 + \alpha_1s + \alpha_0}$.

ask.explanation: The first column of $\mathrm{adj}(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})$ is $[s - a_{22} \;\; a_{21}]^T$ = $[s + {{-a22}} \;\; {{a21}}]^T$. Multiply by $\mathbf{C}$: ${{c1}}(s + {{-a22}}) + ({{c2}})({{a21}})$. The constant term is $\beta_0$ = {{c1*(-a22)}} + ({{c2*a21}}) = {{b0}}.

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{{{D}}s^2 + {{D*a1+b1}}s + {{D*a2+b2}}}{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$ has numerator and denominator of the same degree, so $D \ne 0$. Realize it in control canonical form.

ask.explanation: Divide: $G(s) = D + \frac{b_1s + b_2}{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$. The ratio of the leading coefficients gives $D$ = {{D}}; it is the value of $G$ at very high frequency, the direct feedthrough.
Remainder after removing $D$ = {{D}}: $({{D*a2+b2}} - {{D}}\cdot{{a2}})$ = {{b2}} is the constant term, so $b_2$ = {{b2}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for realizing $G(s) = \frac{6s^2 + 9s + 12}{3s^2 + 3s + 6}$ in control canonical form in order.
items: Divide numerator and denominator by 3 to make the denominator monic
Split off $D = 2$ by polynomial division, leaving the remainder $s + 0$
Put $-1$ and $-2$ in the top row of $\mathbf{A}_c$ and the remainder coefficients $[1 \;\; 0]$ in $\mathbf{C}_c$
steps.explanation: Monic: $\frac{2s^2 + 3s + 4}{s^2 + s + 2}$. Division: $2 + \frac{s + 0}{s^2 + s + 2}$, so $D = 2$. Then $\mathbf{A}_c = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B}_c = [1 \;\; 0]^T$ and $\mathbf{C}_c = [1 \;\; 0]$: the remainder, not the original numerator. Check: $\mathbf{C}_c(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}_c)^{-1}\mathbf{B}_c = \frac{s}{s^2 + s + 2}$, and adding $D = 2$ gives $G(s)$ back.

steps.prompt: Realize $G(s) = \frac{{{b2}}s + {{b3}}}{s^3 + {{a1}}s^2 + {{a2}}s + {{a3}}}$ in control canonical form: $\mathbf{A}_c$ is 3×3, $\mathbf{B}_c = [1 \;\; 0 \;\; 0]^T$, $\mathbf{C}_c = [b_1 \;\; b_2 \;\; b_3]$.

ask.prompt: Find the entry in row 1, column 2 of $\mathbf{A}_c$.
Find the entry in row 1, column 3 of $\mathbf{A}_c$.

ask.explanation: Write the numerator as $b_1s^2 + b_2s + b_3$ = $0\cdot s^2 + {{b2}}s + {{b3}}$. There is no $s^2$ term, so $b_1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{C}_c = [0 \;\; {{b2}} \;\; {{b3}}]$.

steps.prompt: Parallel RLC driven by a current source, with $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $C$ = {{C|F}} and $L$ = {{L|H}}. States $\mathbf{x} = [v_C \;\; i_L]^T$, input $i_s$.

ask.explanation: KCL at the top node: $i_s = \frac{v_C}{R} + C\dot v_C + i_L$, so $\dot v_C = -\frac{1}{RC}v_C - \frac{1}{C}i_L + \frac{1}{C}i_s$. $a_{11} = -\frac{1}{RC}$ = −1/({{R}} × {{C|F}}) = {{-1/(R*C)}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
From KCL, $\dot v_C = -\frac{1}{RC}v_C - \frac{1}{C}i_L + \frac{1}{C}i_s$. $a_{12} = -1/C$ = {{-1/C}} (in V/(A·s)). The inductor current leaves the node, hence the minus sign.
The inductor sees the node voltage: $L\dot i_L = v_C$, so $a_{21} = 1/L$ = {{1/L}} (in A/(V·s)) and $a_{22} = 0$.
The source current flows into the node: $\dot v_C = \ldots + \frac{1}{C}i_s$, so $b_1 = 1/C$ = {{1/C}} (and $b_2 = 0$).

steps.prompt: A circuit contains two capacitors connected **directly in parallel**, a resistor and an inductor. How many state variables does a minimal model need?
steps.explanation: Two capacitors in parallel always share one voltage, so they act as one capacitor $C_1 + C_2$ and give only one independent state. Together with the inductor current that makes 2 states. Counting every energy-storage element (3) gives a model that is not minimal.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a11}} & {{a12}} \\ {{a21}} & {{a22}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [{{c1}} \;\; {{c2}}]$, $D = 0$. $G(s)$ has one zero. Where is it?
steps.explanation: With $\mathbf{B} = [0 \;\; 1]^T$ only the second column of $\mathrm{adj}(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})$ matters: $[a_{12} \;\; s - a_{11}]^T$ = $[{{a12}} \;\; s + {{-a11}}]^T$. The numerator is ${{c1}}\cdot{{a12}} + {{c2}}(s + {{-a11}})$, which is zero at $s = a_{11} - \frac{c_1a_{12}}{c_2}$ = {{a11 - c1*a12/c2}}. The zeros depend on $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, the poles only on $\mathbf{A}$.

steps.prompt: A {{m}} kg mass on a spring ($k$ = {{k}} N/m). The plot shows the eigenvalues of its $\mathbf{A}$ matrix. Set the damper $b$ so that $\mathbf{A}$ has a **double** eigenvalue (critical damping).
steps.explanation: $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = s^2 + \frac{b}{m}s + \frac{k}{m}$. A double root needs a zero discriminant: $\left(\frac{b}{m}\right)^2 = \frac{4k}{m}$, so $b = 2\sqrt{km}$ = 2√({{k}} × {{m}}) = {{bc}} N·s/m. Both eigenvalues then sit at $-\frac{b}{2m}$ = {{-bc/(2*m)}}. Less damping splits them into a complex pair, more damping into two real ones.

steps.prompt: A DC motor with inertia $J$ = {{J}} kg·m², friction $b$ = {{bm}} N·m·s and torque constant $K_t$ = {{Kt}} N·m/A obeys $J\dot\omega = -b\omega + K_ti$. States $\mathbf{x} = [\theta \;\; \omega]^T$, input: the current $i$.

ask.explanation: $\dot\theta = \omega$ gives row 1 = $[0 \;\; 1]$. Row 2: $\dot\omega = -\frac{b}{J}\omega + \frac{K_t}{J}i$, so $a_{22} = -b/J$ = −{{bm}}/{{J}} = {{-bm/J}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
$\dot\omega = -\frac{b}{J}\omega + \frac{K_t}{J}i$, so $b_2 = K_t/J$ = {{Kt}}/{{J}} = {{Kt/J}} (rad/s² per A).

ask.prompt: With the speed as output, $\mathbf{C} = [0 \;\; 1]$, find the DC gain $\omega_{ss}/i$ (in rad/s per A).
ask.explanation: $G(s) = \frac{K_t/J}{s + b/J}$, so $G(0) = \frac{K_t}{b}$ = {{Kt}}/{{bm}} = {{Kt/bm}} rad/s per A. In steady state the motor torque $K_ti$ balances the friction torque $b\omega$.

steps.prompt: Match each system to its natural state variables.
pairs: DC motor driven by a current
steps.explanation: States are the quantities that store energy or matter: electric ($\frac{1}{2}Cv^2$, $\frac{1}{2}Li^2$), mechanical (spring compression and kinetic energy), rotational (angle and $\frac{1}{2}J\omega^2$) and thermal (heat stored as $C_{th}T$). Their initial values determine the future.

steps.prompt: RC ladder with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}, $C_1$ = {{C1|F}}, $C_2$ = {{C2|F}}, output $y = v_2$. Its transfer function is $G(s) = \frac{\alpha_0}{s^2 + \alpha_1s + \alpha_0}$.

ask.explanation: $\alpha_0 = \det\mathbf{A} = \left(\frac{1}{R_1C_1} + \frac{1}{R_2C_1}\right)\frac{1}{R_2C_2}$ $- \frac{1}{R_2C_1}\cdot\frac{1}{R_2C_2} = \frac{1}{R_1R_2C_1C_2}$ = {{1/(R1*R2*C1*C2)}} $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. The numerator is the same number, so the DC gain is 1: at DC no current flows and $v_2 = v_s$.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a11}} & {{a12}} \\ {{a21}} & {{a22}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} {{b1}} \\ {{b2}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [{{c1}} \;\; {{c2}}]$, $D$ = {{D}}. Find the DC gain $G(0)$.
steps.explanation:
At $s = 0$: $G(0) = -\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B} + D$ (the steady state of $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{x}_{ss} = -\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B}u$).
$\det\mathbf{A}$ = ({{a11}})({{a22}}) − ({{a12}})({{a21}}) = {{dt}}, and $\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\det\mathbf{A}}\begin{bmatrix} a_{22}b_1 - a_{12}b_2 \\ a_{11}b_2 - a_{21}b_1 \end{bmatrix}$ = $\frac{1}{ {{dt}} }\begin{bmatrix} {{a22*b1 - a12*b2}} \\ {{a11*b2 - a21*b1}} \end{bmatrix}$.
$G(0)$ = {{D}} − ({{c1}}·({{a22*b1 - a12*b2}}) + ({{c2}})·({{a11*b2 - a21*b1}}))/{{dt}} = {{D - (c1*(a22*b1 - a12*b2) + c2*(a11*b2 - a21*b1))/dt}}.

steps.prompt: Which model does **not** realize $G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}$?
steps.explanation:
Check each one with $\mathbf{C}(s\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B}$:
- Diagonal model: $\frac{1}{s+1} + \frac{1}{s+2} = \frac{2s+3}{(s+1)(s+2)}$. Wrong numerator; $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; -1]$ would have worked.
- Control canonical form of $\frac{0\cdot s + 1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}$: correct.
- Observer canonical form with $\mathbf{B}_o = [0 \;\; 1]^T$: correct.
- Triangular model: $\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}$, correct (the worked example on the study card).

steps.prompt: Realize $G(s) = \frac{{{K}}}{(s+{{p1}})(s+{{p2}})(s+{{p3}})}$ in control canonical form ($\mathbf{B}_c = [1 \;\; 0 \;\; 0]^T$).

ask.prompt: Find the entry in row 1, column 2 of $\mathbf{A}_c$.
Find the entry in row 1, column 3 of $\mathbf{A}_c$.
ask.explanation: The constant term of the denominator is $a_3 = p_1p_2p_3$ = {{p1}}·{{p2}}·{{p3}} = {{p1*p2*p3}}, so the entry is −{{p1*p2*p3}}.
The numerator is $0\cdot s^2 + 0\cdot s + {{K}}$, so $\mathbf{C}_c = [0 \;\; 0 \;\; {{K}}]$: the output is {{K}} times the last state.

steps.prompt: In a series RLC circuit ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $L$ = {{L|H}}, $C$ = {{C|F}}) the output is the resistor voltage, $y = Ri_L$. States $[v_C \;\; i_L]^T$, input $v_s$.

ask.explanation: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{C} \\ -\frac{1}{L} & -\frac{R}{L} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \frac{1}{L} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [0 \;\; R]$. The second column of the adjugate is $[\frac{1}{C} \;\; s]^T$, so the numerator is $R\cdot s\cdot\frac{1}{L}$: $\beta_1 = R/L$ = {{R/L}} $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

$G(s) = \frac{(R/L)s}{s^2 + (R/L)s + 1/(LC)}$. At $s = j\omega_0$ the terms $-\omega_0^2$ and $1/(LC)$ cancel, leaving $\frac{(R/L)j\omega_0}{(R/L)j\omega_0} = 1$. At resonance the $L$ and $C$ impedances cancel and the whole source voltage appears across $R$: a band-pass filter.

steps.prompt: If $D \ne 0$, the output of a state model that starts at $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{0}$ jumps at $t = 0^+$ when a unit step is applied to $u$.
steps.explanation: $y(0^+) = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}(0^+) + Du(0^+)$. The states come out of integrators and cannot jump, so $\mathbf{x}(0^+) = \mathbf{0}$, but $Du$ jumps from 0 to $D$. In transfer-function terms: $G(\infty) = D \ne 0$, a biproper $G(s)$ with as many zeros as poles.
